questions.title: Nerve supply of the upper lateral eyelid skin
questions.question: Skin over the upper lateral eyelid is supplied by the:

explanations.A: Correct. The lacrimal nerve is the most lateral branch of the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve; after running along the upper border of lateral rectus and through the lacrimal gland, its terminal cutaneous twigs supply the skin of the upper eyelid's lateral part and adjoining conjunctiva. This lateral position, distinct from the more medial frontal-nerve branches, is exactly what makes it the answer for the LATERAL upper eyelid specifically.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The supraorbital nerve (a frontal nerve branch of V1) supplies the skin of the upper eyelid's medial/central part, forehead and scalp — the middle of the eyelid, not its lateral part.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The supratrochlear nerve (also a frontal nerve branch of V1) supplies the skin near the medial angle of the eye and lower medial forehead — the medial, not lateral, side.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The zygomaticofacial nerve (a branch of the zygomatic nerve, V2/maxillary division) supplies skin over the zygomatic (cheek) prominence, below and lateral to the eye — not the eyelid itself.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the lacrimal nerve (V1) as supplying skin of the upper LATERAL eyelid, distinguishing it from the more medial supraorbital/supratrochlear branches and from the zygomaticofacial nerve's cheek territory.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Orbit and Eyelid > Ophthalmic Nerve Cutaneous Branches

questions.title: Effect of a stab wound in the submandibular triangle
questions.question: Stab wound directed into submandibular triangle may lead to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ptosis follows sympathetic chain or oculomotor nerve injury in the neck/orbit region, not a structure that runs through the submandibular triangle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Drop of the shoulder follows accessory nerve (CN XI) injury, which crosses the POSTERIOR triangle of the neck, not the submandibular triangle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Deviation of the mouth follows facial nerve (CN VII) injury; the facial nerve's cervical branch does cross near this region but the submandibular triangle's most exposed named nerve is the hypoglossal, not the facial trunk.
explanations.D: Correct. The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) loops through the floor of the submandibular triangle on its way to the tongue, making it the structure most vulnerable to a penetrating stab wound there. Hypoglossal nerve injury paralyses the ipsilateral genioglossus and related tongue muscles. The tongue's own unopposed contralateral muscles then push it over toward the injured side on protrusion, producing the deviation this option describes.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the hypoglossal nerve as the structure most at risk in the submandibular triangle, and tongue deviation as the resulting sign of its injury.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Neck > Submandibular Triangle

questions.title: Facial nerve exit from the skull
questions.question: The facial nerve:

options.A: Marginal mandibular branch supplies muscles of the upper and lower lips
options.C: Has four main branches that exit the parotid gland
options.D: Supplies the anterior belly of digastric

explanations.A: Incorrect. The marginal mandibular branch supplies the muscles of the LOWER lip only (depressor labii inferioris, depressor anguli oris, mentalis) — the upper lip is supplied by the buccal and zygomatic branches instead.
explanations.B: Correct. After leaving the brainstem and traversing the facial canal within the temporal bone, the facial nerve exits the skull through the stylomastoid foramen, immediately posterior to the styloid process, before entering the parotid gland and dividing into its terminal branches. This exit point also explains the classic surgical landmark: a parotid or mastoid-region approach must identify the nerve as it emerges here before it fans out into its branches within the gland.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The facial nerve classically divides into FIVE terminal branches (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical) within the parotid gland, not four.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The facial nerve supplies the POSTERIOR belly of digastric (via its digastric branch); the anterior belly of digastric is supplied by the mylohyoid nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3).

questions.learning_objective: State that the facial nerve exits the skull through the stylomastoid foramen before entering the parotid gland.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Cranial Nerves > Facial Nerve

questions.title: Muscle supplied by the abducent nerve
questions.question: The Abducent nerve supplies the ___ muscle:

explanations.A: Correct. The abducent nerve (CN VI) supplies a single extraocular muscle, lateral rectus, which abducts the eye (turns it laterally) — the nerve's own name reflects this single, specific action. Because only one muscle is involved, an isolated abducent nerve palsy produces a pure horizontal deviation (a medially deviated, non-abducting eye) without affecting elevation, depression or lid position.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Superior tarsal (Müller's) muscle is smooth muscle supplied by sympathetic fibres, not the abducent nerve.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Superior rectus is supplied by the oculomotor nerve (CN III), not the abducent nerve.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inferior oblique is also supplied by the oculomotor nerve (CN III), not the abducent nerve.

questions.learning_objective: State that the abducent nerve supplies lateral rectus only, distinguishing it from the oculomotor-supplied extraocular muscles.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Cranial Nerves > Abducent Nerve

questions.title: Muscle that opens the jaw
questions.question: Which muscle helps to open the jaw?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Medial pterygoid is a muscle of MASTICATION that elevates (closes) the mandible and assists in protrusion, not opening.
explanations.B: Correct. Lateral pterygoid is the only one of the four muscles of mastication that acts to open (depress) the mandible, by pulling the condyle and articular disc forward as the mouth opens; the other three (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid) all elevate/close the jaw. This is why a lateral pterygoid palsy classically causes the jaw to deviate TOWARD the weak side on opening, since the healthy contralateral muscle pulls the mandible over unopposed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Masseter is a powerful jaw-CLOSING (elevator) muscle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Temporalis is also a jaw-CLOSING (elevator) muscle, with its posterior fibres additionally retracting the mandible.

questions.learning_objective: Identify lateral pterygoid as the jaw-opening muscle among the four muscles of mastication, the other three being elevators.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Muscles of Mastication

questions.title: Origin of the inferior root of the ansa cervicalis
questions.question: Inferior root of ansa cervicalis is derived from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. C1 (via the hypoglossal nerve) forms the SUPERIOR root (descendens hypoglossi) of the ansa cervicalis, not the inferior root.
explanations.B: Correct. The inferior root of the ansa cervicalis (descendens cervicalis) arises directly from the C2 and C3 anterior rami of the cervical plexus, descending to join the superior root and complete the ansa (loop), which then supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles. This inferior root's fibres travel down from the cervical plexus independently of the hypoglossal nerve itself, only joining it functionally within the ansa loop.
explanations.C: Incorrect. C4 and C5 are not the source of either root of the ansa cervicalis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. C6 and C7 are not the source of either root of the ansa cervicalis.

questions.learning_objective: State that the ansa cervicalis's inferior root (descendens cervicalis) arises from C2 and C3, while the superior root arises via C1 through the hypoglossal nerve.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Neck > Ansa Cervicalis

questions.title: Muscle dividing the posterior triangle
questions.question: The posterior triangle is divided into two triangles by ___ muscle:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Digastric's posterior belly helps bound the ANTERIOR triangle (forming its digastric/submandibular subdivision), not the posterior triangle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Trapezius forms the posterior BORDER of the posterior triangle as a whole, rather than subdividing it.
explanations.C: Correct. The inferior belly of omohyoid crosses the posterior triangle and divides it into a larger occipital triangle (above) and a smaller, more inferior subclavian (supraclavicular) triangle (below). This landmark distinction matters clinically because the subclavian (supraclavicular) triangle below omohyoid is where the subclavian artery and brachial plexus trunks are surgically accessed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mylohyoid forms the floor of the mouth and helps bound the submental triangle, unrelated to the posterior triangle's subdivision.

questions.learning_objective: State that omohyoid's inferior belly subdivides the posterior triangle into occipital and subclavian (supraclavicular) triangles.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Neck > Triangles of the Neck > Posterior Triangle

questions.title: Location of the maxillary sinus hiatus
questions.question: A 54-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with severe pain in his nasal cavity. Radiographic examination reveals a carcinoma in his nasal cavity. In which of the following locations would the carcinoma block the hiatus of the maxillary sinus?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The inferior meatus receives the opening of the nasolacrimal duct, not the maxillary sinus.
explanations.B: Correct. The maxillary sinus drains through its ostium into the hiatus semilunaris, a groove located in the MIDDLE meatus of the lateral nasal wall (alongside the frontal and anterior ethmoidal sinus openings); a tumour obstructing this region blocks maxillary sinus drainage. Because the frontal and anterior ethmoidal sinuses also drain into this same region, a middle-meatus obstruction from tumour or polyp can block multiple sinuses' outflow at once, not the maxillary sinus alone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superior meatus receives drainage from the posterior ethmoidal air cells, not the maxillary sinus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The nasopharynx lies posterior to the nasal cavity proper and is not where any paranasal sinus drains.

questions.learning_objective: Localise the maxillary sinus's drainage ostium (hiatus semilunaris) to the middle meatus of the lateral nasal wall.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Nose and Paranasal Sinuses > Maxillary Sinus

questions.title: Dural venous sinus closest to the pituitary gland
questions.question: A 37-year-old patient has an infectious inflammation of the dural venous sinus closest to the pituitary gland and a secondary thrombus formation. Which of the following is the most likely site of infection?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The straight sinus runs in the midline where the falx cerebri meets the tentorium cerebelli, well away from the pituitary fossa.
explanations.B: Correct. The cavernous sinus lies directly lateral to the pituitary gland and sphenoid sinus, making it the dural venous sinus closest to the pituitary; it is a well-known site of septic thrombosis (cavernous sinus thrombosis), classically spreading from facial or sinus infection via the valveless facial/ophthalmic venous connections. Because the cavernous sinus receives the ophthalmic veins and drains the facial venous plexus, infection can spread there directly from a facial or orbital source via these valveless connections.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superior petrosal sinus drains the cavernous sinus into the transverse sinus along the petrous temporal bone's superior border — adjacent to, but not itself the sinus closest to, the pituitary.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The sigmoid sinus lies in the posterior cranial fossa, continuing from the transverse sinus toward the jugular foramen, far from the pituitary fossa.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the cavernous sinus as the dural venous sinus adjacent to the pituitary gland and the classic site of septic sinus thrombosis.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Cranial Venous Sinuses > Cavernous Sinus

questions.title: Muscle forming the oral diaphragm
questions.question: Which one of the following muscles forms the diaphragm of the oral cavity?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Digastric's two bellies bound the submandibular and submental triangles but do not themselves form a continuous sheet across the floor of the mouth.
explanations.B: Correct. Mylohyoid is a paired, flat muscle whose fibres meet in a median raphe to form a muscular sling that is literally called the 'diaphragm of the oral cavity' — the floor of the mouth, supporting the tongue and submandibular structures above it. Its median raphe and lateral attachment to the mylohyoid line of the mandible give it the sling-like shape needed to support the tongue and floor structures above it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Geniohyoid lies ABOVE mylohyoid (deep to it) and elevates the hyoid bone/depresses the mandible; it does not itself form the floor sheet.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Stylohyoid is a slender muscle running from the styloid process to the hyoid bone, unrelated to forming the floor of the mouth.

questions.learning_objective: Identify mylohyoid as the muscular diaphragm of the oral cavity (floor of the mouth).
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Floor of Mouth

questions.title: Little's area location
questions.question: The common site of nose bleeding (Little's area) is located at which part of the nose.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The roof of the nasal cavity is formed by the cribriform plate region and is not the site of Little's area.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The floor of the nasal cavity (formed by the hard palate) is not the site of Little's area.
explanations.C: Correct. Little's area is a vascular plexus (Kiesselbach's plexus) on the ANTERIOR part of the nasal SEPTUM, where branches of the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial arteries anastomose superficially — the commonest site of epistaxis (nosebleed) because of this dense, exposed anastomotic network. Because these vessels sit superficially just beneath the septal mucosa with little protective tissue, even minor trauma (nose-picking, dry air, a blow) readily ruptures them.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lateral wall (with its conchae/meatuses) is not the site of Little's area, and the question does not specify a side-restricted lesion.

questions.learning_objective: Localise Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus), the commonest site of epistaxis, to the anterior nasal septum.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Nose > Nasal Septum

questions.title: Branch of the carotid artery
questions.question: Branches of the carotid artery include:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery, not the carotid artery.
explanations.B: Correct. The ascending pharyngeal artery is one of the named branches of the external carotid artery (its smallest and most posteromedial branch), supplying the pharyngeal wall, prevertebral muscles and part of the middle ear/meninges. The external carotid's other named branches — superior thyroid, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, superficial temporal and maxillary — are the usual distractors in this kind of question, none of which the printed options here reproduce correctly.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery is a branch of the subclavian artery, not the carotid artery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superficial cervical artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery, not the carotid artery.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the ascending pharyngeal artery as an external carotid branch, distinguishing it from subclavian/thyrocervical-trunk branches.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Neck > Carotid Arteries
questions.subtopic: Vasculature of the head and neck

questions.title: Origin of the middle meningeal artery
questions.question: The middle meningeal artery is a branch of the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The internal carotid artery does not give rise to the middle meningeal artery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The middle cerebral artery is an intracranial branch of the internal carotid supplying brain tissue, unrelated to the middle meningeal artery.
explanations.C: Correct. The middle meningeal artery arises from the maxillary artery (the largest terminal branch of the external carotid artery), entering the skull through the foramen spinosum to supply the dura mater and calvaria — clinically important as the vessel classically torn in extradural (epidural) haemorrhage. This course through bone rather than soft tissue is exactly why a skull fracture crossing the pterion can lacerate the artery and produce a rapidly expanding extradural haematoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The deep temporal arteries are separate maxillary artery branches supplying temporalis muscle, not the source of the middle meningeal artery.

questions.learning_objective: State that the middle meningeal artery is a branch of the maxillary artery, entering the skull via foramen spinosum.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Skull and Meninges > Middle Meningeal Artery

questions.title: Palatal muscle innervated by the trigeminal nerve
questions.question: Which one of the following muscles of the palate is innervated by the trigeminal nerve?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Palatoglossus is innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (vagal fibres via CN X), not the trigeminal nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Musculus uvulae is innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (vagal fibres via CN X), not the trigeminal nerve.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Palatopharyngeus is innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (vagal fibres via CN X), not the trigeminal nerve.
explanations.D: Correct. Tensor veli palatini is the sole exception among the palate muscles: it is supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3, via the nerve to medial pterygoid), while every other palatal muscle (levator veli palatini, palatoglossus, palatopharyngeus, musculus uvulae) is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus. This exception is a favourite exam distinction precisely because every other palate muscle breaks the same rule, making tensor veli palatini easy to test as the odd one out.

questions.learning_objective: Identify tensor veli palatini as the one palate muscle supplied by the trigeminal nerve (V3), all others being pharyngeal-plexus (vagal).
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Pharynx and Palate > Muscles of the Soft Palate

questions.title: Nerve injury after tonsillectomy causing posterior tongue taste loss
questions.question: After having a tonsillectomy, a 57-year-old man with a long history of chewing tobacco use is unable to detect taste on the posterior one-third of his tongue. Which of the following nerves has most likely been injured?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The internal laryngeal nerve carries sensation above the vocal folds within the larynx, not taste from the tongue.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lingual nerve (CN V3) carries general sensation from the ANTERIOR two-thirds of the tongue, and taste there travels via the chorda tympani riding on it — the posterior third is a different nerve's territory entirely.
explanations.C: Correct. The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) runs close to the tonsillar bed (the tonsillar fossa lies against the pharyngeal wall the nerve crosses) and is the recognised nerve at risk during tonsillectomy; it supplies both general sensation AND taste to the posterior one-third of the tongue, so its injury selectively abolishes taste there while sparing the anterior two-thirds (chorda tympani/facial nerve territory). Because both general sensation and taste from the posterior third travel together in CN IX, a single nerve injury here explains the isolated finding without needing to invoke a second nerve.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The greater palatine nerve supplies the hard palate mucosa, not tongue taste.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise glossopharyngeal nerve injury during tonsillectomy as the cause of isolated posterior-tongue taste loss, distinguishing its territory from the lingual/chorda tympani's anterior two-thirds.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Cranial Nerves > Glossopharyngeal Nerve

questions.title: Nerve injured given the direction of tongue deviation
questions.question: Following a penetrated injury in the submandibular triangle, the tongue of a 45-year-old patient deviates to the left on protrusion. Which of the following nerves is injured?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lingual nerve injury affects general sensation (and, via chorda tympani, taste) of the tongue's anterior two-thirds, not the genioglossus muscle that steers the tongue during protrusion — it does not cause deviation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lingual nerve injury does not cause tongue deviation on protrusion, regardless of side, because it carries sensory rather than motor fibres to genioglossus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Injury to the RIGHT hypoglossal nerve would weaken the RIGHT genioglossus, causing the tongue to deviate to the RIGHT (the injured side), not the left as described here.
explanations.D: Correct. On protrusion, genioglossus on each side pulls the tongue forward and slightly to the opposite side; healthy bilateral genioglossus balances this out to straight protrusion. When one hypoglossal nerve is injured, the unopposed healthy-side genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the WEAK (injured) side — so left-ward deviation on protrusion localises the lesion to the left hypoglossal nerve.

questions.learning_objective: Infer that the tongue deviates toward the side of a hypoglossal nerve injury on protrusion, and use this to localise the injured nerve from the direction of deviation.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Cranial Nerves > Hypoglossal Nerve

questions.title: Vein alongside the deep cervical lymph nodes
questions.question: The deep cervical lymph nodes are located alongside the ___ vein:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The subclavian vein is not the vessel the deep cervical nodal chain runs alongside.
explanations.B: Correct. The deep cervical lymph nodes form a chain running the length of the neck alongside the internal jugular vein, within the carotid sheath, receiving drainage from the superficial cervical nodes and from most head-and-neck structures before draining into the jugular lymphatic trunk. Because this chain drains almost the entire head and neck before lymph reaches the venous system, palpating nodes along the internal jugular vein is a core part of the head-and-neck clinical examination.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The external jugular vein runs alongside the SUPERFICIAL cervical lymph nodes, not the deep chain.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anterior jugular vein is a small superficial vein unrelated to the deep cervical nodal chain.

questions.learning_objective: State that the deep cervical lymph nodes lie alongside the internal jugular vein, distinguishing them from the superficial chain along the external jugular vein.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Neck > Lymphatic Drainage

questions.title: Pharyngeal muscle from the pterygomandibular raphe
questions.question: The pharyngeal muscle that originates from the pterygomandibular raphe is the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Stylopharyngeus arises from the styloid process of the temporal bone, not the pterygomandibular raphe.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Middle constrictor arises from the stylohyoid ligament and the hyoid bone (greater and lesser horns), not the pterygomandibular raphe.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Palatopharyngeus arises from the palatine aponeurosis of the soft palate, not the pterygomandibular raphe.
explanations.D: Correct. The superior constrictor arises in part from the pterygomandibular raphe — the fibrous band stretching between the pterygoid hamulus above and the posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible below — along with the medial pterygoid plate, pterygoid hamulus and mandible itself. The raphe itself is not attached to bone along most of its length, which is why the superior constrictor's origin here is described as a fibrous line rather than a bony ridge.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the superior constrictor as the pharyngeal constrictor that originates in part from the pterygomandibular raphe.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Pharynx > Pharyngeal Constrictors

questions.title: Wall of the middle ear formed by the tympanic membrane
questions.question: The tympanic membrane is at the ___ wall of the middle ear:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The medial wall of the middle ear is formed by the promontory (basal turn of the cochlea) and the oval/round windows, not the tympanic membrane.
explanations.B: Correct. The tympanic membrane forms almost the entire LATERAL wall of the middle ear (tympanic) cavity, separating it from the external acoustic meatus and transmitting sound vibrations to the ossicular chain. This lateral position is what allows otoscopic examination to visualise the membrane directly from the external ear canal, and why a perforation here connects the middle ear cavity to the outside.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The inferior wall (floor) of the middle ear relates to the jugular bulb, not the tympanic membrane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anterior wall of the middle ear carries the opening of the pharyngotympanic (Eustachian) tube, not the tympanic membrane.

questions.learning_objective: State that the tympanic membrane forms the lateral wall of the middle ear cavity.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Ear > Middle Ear

questions.title: Function of the internal laryngeal nerve
questions.question: The internal laryngeal nerve supplies:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sensation AT and below the level of the vocal folds is carried by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, not the internal laryngeal nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cricothyroid is supplied by the EXTERNAL laryngeal nerve (a motor branch of the superior laryngeal nerve), not the internal laryngeal nerve, which is purely sensory.
explanations.C: Correct. The internal laryngeal nerve (the sensory branch of the superior laryngeal nerve) pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and supplies sensation to the laryngeal mucosa ABOVE the vocal folds, down to their upper surface — the mucosa at and below the folds is instead supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. This sensory/motor split across the two superior laryngeal nerve branches is exactly why superior laryngeal nerve injury classically causes reduced laryngeal sensation above the folds together with reduced pitch, rather than airway obstruction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. All the intrinsic muscles of the larynx except cricothyroid (including transverse arytenoid) are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, a motor nerve — not the purely sensory internal laryngeal nerve.

questions.learning_objective: State that the internal laryngeal nerve is purely sensory, supplying laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds, distinguishing it from the motor external and recurrent laryngeal nerves.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Larynx > Laryngeal Nerve Supply

questions.title: Tongue muscle supplied by the pharyngeal plexus
questions.question: The ___ muscle of the tongue is innervated by the pharyngeal plexus:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hyoglossus, like almost all other tongue muscles, is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), not the pharyngeal plexus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Styloglossus is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), not the pharyngeal plexus.
explanations.C: Correct. Palatoglossus is the single exception among the tongue's muscles: although it acts on the tongue, it is developmentally a palatal muscle and is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagal fibres, CN X) rather than the hypoglossal nerve, which supplies every other tongue muscle (extrinsic and intrinsic). This split explains why an isolated vagal lesion affecting the pharyngeal plexus can weaken palatoglossus specifically while every other tongue muscle, still supplied by an intact hypoglossal nerve, stays unaffected.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The intrinsic vertical (and all other intrinsic) tongue muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), not the pharyngeal plexus.

questions.learning_objective: Identify palatoglossus as the one tongue muscle supplied by the pharyngeal plexus rather than the hypoglossal nerve.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Tongue > Tongue Muscles

questions.title: Triangle between the anterior bellies of digastric
questions.question: Which triangle of the neck lies between the anterior bellies of digastric muscles?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The occipital triangle is the upper subdivision of the posterior triangle, unrelated to the digastric muscles.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posterior triangle lies behind sternocleidomastoid and is bounded by trapezius, not by the digastric bellies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The muscular (inferior carotid) triangle is bounded by omohyoid, sternocleidomastoid and the midline, not the digastric bellies.
explanations.D: Correct. The submental triangle is bounded by the anterior belly of digastric on each side and the hyoid bone below, with the midline symphysis menti above — it lies directly between the two anterior digastric bellies. This triangle contains the submental lymph nodes and small submental veins, making it a relevant surgical landmark for floor-of-mouth and anterior tongue drainage.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the submental triangle as the neck triangle bounded by the two anterior bellies of digastric.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Neck > Triangles of the Neck > Submental Triangle

questions.title: Muscle responsible for ptosis when its smooth part is paralysed
questions.question: Ptosis (dropping of the upper eyelid) is due to paralysis of the smooth muscle part of the ___ muscle:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Superior rectus is an extraocular muscle that elevates the globe; it has no eyelid-elevating smooth-muscle component.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Superior oblique is an extraocular muscle that depresses/rotates the globe, unrelated to eyelid elevation.
explanations.C: Correct. Levator palpebrae superioris has two parts: a voluntary skeletal-muscle component (oculomotor nerve, CN III) providing most eyelid elevation, and a smooth-muscle component — the superior tarsal muscle (Müller's muscle) — supplied by sympathetic fibres, which provides the extra few millimetres of lid elevation. Loss of sympathetic supply paralyses this smooth part specifically, producing the mild ptosis classically seen in Horner's syndrome (as opposed to the complete ptosis of an oculomotor nerve palsy, which paralyses the skeletal part instead).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Depressor anguli oris is a muscle of facial expression around the mouth, unrelated to the eyelid.

questions.learning_objective: Identify levator palpebrae superioris's smooth-muscle part (superior tarsal/Müller's muscle, sympathetically supplied) as the structure whose paralysis produces ptosis, e.g. in Horner's syndrome.

questions.title: Ligament thickening the investing layer of deep cervical fascia
questions.question: Which one of the following ligaments is a thickened part of investing layer of the deep cervical fascia?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Thyrohyoid" names a membrane connecting the thyroid cartilage and hyoid bone, not a thickening of the investing fascia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The supraspinous ligament belongs to the vertebral column (running along the tips of the vertebral spinous processes), unrelated to cervical fascia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cricothyroid ligament connects the cricoid and thyroid cartilages of the larynx, not a thickening of the investing fascia.
explanations.D: Correct. The stylomandibular ligament is a discrete thickened band of the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, running from the styloid process to the angle of the mandible and separating the parotid and submandibular salivary gland beds. This anatomical relationship is why the ligament helps keep abscesses or tumours confined to one side, rarely spreading directly between the parotid and submandibular spaces.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the stylomandibular ligament as a thickened part of the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, separating the parotid and submandibular gland beds.

questions.title: Muscle that rotates the face upward and to the left
questions.question: Moving the head so that the face looks upwards and to the left is a movement produced by the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Platysma is a thin subcutaneous muscle of facial expression/neck skin tension, not a mover of head rotation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Trapezius contributes to head/neck extension and, with sternocleidomastoid, to rotation, but acting alone on the LEFT it does not produce this specific upward-and-left-facing turn the way the paired sternocleidomastoid action does.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Geniohyoid elevates the hyoid bone/depresses the mandible and plays no role in turning the head.
explanations.D: Correct. Each sternocleidomastoid rotates the face toward the OPPOSITE side while tilting the head toward its OWN side, and (acting with the extensor group) assists in extending/tilting the head upward; a single right sternocleidomastoid contraction therefore turns the face to the left and helps tip the head up, matching this described movement. This paired, opposite-side rotation action is why testing sternocleidomastoid strength — turning the head against resistance — evaluates the accessory nerve on the side OPPOSITE to the direction the patient turns.

questions.learning_objective: State that unilateral sternocleidomastoid contraction rotates the face to the OPPOSITE side (right SCM turns the face left) while tilting the head to its own side.

questions.title: Nerve supplying skin over the angle of the mandible
questions.question: A patient had lost cutaneous sensation over the angle of the mandible, which nerve is most likely damaged?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The mandibular nerve (CN V3) supplies skin over the lower face/jaw via its own branches, but the specific patch of skin overlying the angle of the mandible and the parotid/lower ear region is instead supplied by a cervical plexus branch, not the trigeminal mandibular division.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ophthalmic nerve (CN V1) supplies the forehead, upper eyelid and nose — nowhere near the angle of the mandible.
explanations.C: Correct. The great auricular nerve, a branch of the cervical plexus (C2, C3) that ascends over sternocleidomastoid, supplies skin over the angle of the mandible, parotid gland region and lower auricle — its territory is exactly the area described, making it the classic answer for sensory loss here. This is also why great auricular nerve injury during parotidectomy, where it lies superficially and is at particular surgical risk, produces numbness over the parotid region and mandibular angle rather than the mouth or upper face.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The auriculotemporal nerve (a branch of CN V3) supplies skin over the temporal region and anterior/superior auricle, adjacent to but not covering the angle of the mandible itself.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the great auricular nerve (cervical plexus, C2-C3) as supplying skin over the angle of the mandible, distinguishing its territory from the trigeminal nerve's.
